questions.stem: In the sentence "The man who repaired our generator lives in Aba", the word *who* is which kind of pronoun?
questions.explanation: A relative pronoun introduces a clause that describes a noun already mentioned. Here *who* introduces "who repaired our generator", which tells us more about *the man*. The sentence is a statement, not a question, so *who* is relative rather than interrogative.

distractorRationale.a: *Who* is interrogative only when it actually asks a question, as in "Who repaired the generator?"
distractorRationale.c: Demonstrative pronouns point things out: this, that, these, those
distractorRationale.d: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and refer back to the subject

questions.stem: In the sentence "These are the books I ordered from Onitsha", the word *These* is which kind of pronoun?
questions.explanation: A demonstrative pronoun points out which things are meant — this and that for one item, these and those for more than one. Here *These* stands alone as the subject of the sentence, so it is a pronoun rather than a determiner. In "These books are new", the same word would be a demonstrative adjective because it modifies *books*.

distractorRationale.a: Indefinite pronouns such as someone, anything and few do not point to specific items
distractorRationale.b: Possessive pronouns are mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs
distractorRationale.d: There is a relative pronoun understood before *I ordered*, namely *that*, but *These* is not it

questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: "Between you and ______, the arrangement was unfair."
questions.explanation: *Between* is a preposition, and every pronoun that follows a preposition must be in the objective case. The objective form of *I* is *me*, so the correct expression is "between you and me". The fact that another pronoun, *you*, comes first changes nothing.

distractorRationale.a: Uses the subjective case; students choose *I* because it sounds more polished, but no subject is needed after a preposition
distractorRationale.c: A reflexive pronoun is used only when the subject and the object are the same person
distractorRationale.d: *Mine* is possessive and would mean 'the thing belonging to me'

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence in Standard formal English: "It was ______ who reported the matter to the police."
questions.explanation: After the linking verb *was*, the pronoun is a complement, not an object, and a complement takes the subjective case. You can confirm it by noting that the pronoun is also the subject of the following clause *who reported the matter*, so it must be *he*.

distractorRationale.a: Uses the objective case, which is common in speech but not accepted as formal written English here
distractorRationale.c: *His* is possessive and cannot serve as the subject of *reported*
distractorRationale.d: A reflexive pronoun needs a matching subject earlier in the clause, and there is none

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence in Standard formal English: "My elder brother is much taller than ______."
questions.explanation: In formal English *than* introduces a shortened clause, so the full sentence is "taller than I am". Because the pronoun is the subject of the understood verb *am*, it takes the subjective form *I*. Restoring the missing verb is the quickest way to test any comparison of this kind.

distractorRationale.a: Treats *than* as a preposition; this is normal in casual speech but is marked wrong in formal exam usage
distractorRationale.c: *Mine* would compare my brother with something I own rather than with me
distractorRationale.d: Reflexives cannot appear in a comparison with no matching subject

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Each of the girls in the hostel has ______ own reading lamp."
questions.explanation: The subject is *Each*, which is singular, so the pronoun that refers back to it must also be singular. Since the girls are female, the singular possessive is *her*. The plural noun *girls* inside the phrase *of the girls* is not the antecedent; it is only part of a modifying phrase.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with *girls* instead of with the real antecedent *Each*
distractorRationale.c: *Theirs* is a plural possessive pronoun and cannot stand before the noun *own reading lamp*
distractorRationale.d: *Hers* is a possessive pronoun that stands alone; before a noun you need the determiner *her*

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Neither of the two boys has finished ______ assignment."
questions.explanation: *Neither* means 'not one of the two', so it is singular — which is also why the verb is *has* rather than *have*. The pronoun referring back to it must therefore be the singular *his*, since both people involved are boys.

distractorRationale.a: Matches the nearby plural *boys* rather than the singular subject *Neither*
distractorRationale.c: *Theirs* is both plural and unable to stand in front of a noun
distractorRationale.d: *Its* refers to things or animals, not to people

questions.stem: In Standard English, the sentence "Myself and my brother travelled to Jos last week" is correct.
questions.explanation: False. A reflexive pronoun such as *myself* can never be the subject of a sentence; it is used only when the subject and object are the same person, as in "I hurt myself". The correct subject form is "My brother and I travelled to Jos last week", with the other person named first out of courtesy.

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The candidate ______ the panel recommended has been offered the post."
questions.explanation: Inside the relative clause, *the panel* is the subject and *recommended* is the verb, so the pronoun is the object of *recommended* — the panel recommended **him**. An object takes the objective form, which is *whom*. The substitution test is reliable: if *him* or *her* fits, use *whom*; if *he* or *she* fits, use *who*.

distractorRationale.a: Uses the subjective case, but the clause already has a subject in *the panel*
distractorRationale.c: *Whose* shows possession, and nothing here belongs to the candidate
distractorRationale.d: *Which* refers to things and animals, never to a person

questions.stem: In the sentence "After the match, the two teams congratulated each other warmly", the expression *each other* is which kind of pronoun?
questions.explanation: A reciprocal pronoun shows that an action passes both ways between two or more parties: *each other* for two, *one another* for more than two. Here each team congratulated the other, so the action is mutual. A reflexive pronoun would instead mean each team congratulated only itself.

distractorRationale.a: Reflexives end in -self or -selves and turn the action back on a single subject
distractorRationale.c: Indefinite pronouns such as somebody or few refer to unspecified people or amounts
distractorRationale.d: Distributives such as each, either and neither pick out members of a group singly rather than showing mutual action

questions.stem: In the sentence 'She bought herself a new dress', the word 'herself' is an example of which kind of pronoun?
questions.explanation: 'Herself' is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the subject 'She'. Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and object of the sentence are the same person or thing.

distractorRationale.a: Demonstrative pronouns point to specific things but do not refer back to the subject.
distractorRationale.c: Indefinite pronouns refer to non-specific persons or things.
distractorRationale.d: Relative pronouns introduce relative clauses but do not serve the reflexive function.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a personal pronoun?
questions.explanation: The word 'They' is a personal pronoun that refers to a specific group of people. Personal pronouns are used to replace specific nouns in a sentence.

distractorRationale.b: Whom is a relative pronoun used to refer to people in relative clauses.
distractorRationale.c: Each is an indefinite pronoun that refers to individual members of a group.
distractorRationale.d: This is a demonstrative pronoun that points to a specific noun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct pronoun to complete the sentence: 'Neither of the students completed _____ assignment on time.'

distractorRationale.b: Their is plural and does not agree with the singular subject 'Neither'.
distractorRationale.c: Its is used for non-human nouns and does not fit the context here.
distractorRationale.d: Her is also singular but does not agree with the masculine context of the students.

distractorRationale.c: Demonstrative pronouns point to specific nouns rather than connecting clauses.

distractorRationale.a: Their is plural and does not agree with the singular 'Everyone'.

distractorRationale.d: Them is a plural pronoun and does not match the singular subject.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses pronouns correctly?

options.text: Me and my sister went to the market.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'They invited us to their party.' uses pronouns correctly. 'They' is the subject pronoun and 'us' is the object pronoun that agrees with 'they'.

distractorRationale.a: Me should be replaced with 'My sister and I' for correct subject pronoun usage.
distractorRationale.b: She should be replaced with 'her' to match the object position.
distractorRationale.d: Him should be replaced with 'He' to correctly use the subject pronoun.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is correct in terms of pronoun usage?

options.text: Each of the players have their own jersey.
Everyone should take care of their belongings.
Neither of the answers are correct.
All of the children brought his or her lunch.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'Everyone should take care of their belongings.' is correct because 'their' is commonly accepted as a singular, gender-neutral pronoun in modern usage.

distractorRationale.a: Have should be changed to 'has' for agreement with the singular subject 'Each'.
distractorRationale.c: Are should be changed to 'is' for agreement with the singular subject 'Neither'.
distractorRationale.d: His or her is correct, but 'All' is plural, so 'their' would be more appropriate.
